questions.q: Why doesn't SOQL support an arbitrary JOIN keyword like T-SQL does?
options: SOQL only lets you traverse predefined relationships Salesforce already knows about, not join any two objects on an arbitrary condition
JOIN exists in SOQL but uses different keyword capitalization
SOQL doesn't support relationships between objects at all
SOQL requires a stored procedure to perform any join
questions.explain: SOQL has no JOIN keyword — relationships must already exist (e.g. a lookup field), traversed via dot notation or nested queries, the subject of Chapter 3.

questions.q: How does SOQL handle changing data (updating, deleting, or inserting records)?
options: SOQL UPDATE and DELETE statements work identically to T-SQL
It doesn't — SOQL is read-only; changes go through a separate DML layer via Apex, the API, Data Loader, or Workbench
Only INSERT is supported in SOQL, not UPDATE or DELETE
Data changes require writing the query in all uppercase
questions.explain: SOQL is a read-only query language; DML (Data Manipulation Language) is a separate mechanism entirely.

questions.q: What is a Salesforce governor limit, per this lesson?
options: A limit only on the number of custom objects an org can create
A deprecated Salesforce feature no longer enforced
A hard platform cap, such as on the number of rows a query can return without special handling, that protects shared multi-tenant infrastructure
A setting an admin can freely disable for any org
questions.explain: Governor limits are hard caps that keep any one operation from degrading the shared, multi-tenant Salesforce platform.

questions.q: Why is SELECT * permanently unavailable in SOQL, rather than just an unsupported edge case?
options: It will be added in a future Salesforce release
It works but returns fields in a random, unpredictable order
It only fails when querying custom objects, not standard ones
It's a deliberate, permanent design choice tied to API cost and governor limits, requiring every field to be named explicitly
questions.explain: The lesson states this is permanent by design, not a missing feature — tied directly to API cost and governor limits.

questions.q: In SELECT Name, Account.Industry FROM Opportunity, why is this valid even though SOQL has no JOIN keyword?
options: Opportunity has a predefined relationship to Account through a lookup field, so the relationship can be traversed with dot notation
Account and Opportunity are secretly the same object internally
SOQL treats every object as automatically related to every other object
This query is actually invalid SOQL and would fail
questions.explain: This works only because of Opportunity's predefined AccountId relationship — you still can't join two unrelated objects on an arbitrary condition.
